name: Maya blue and Maya red pigments

image.caption: Maya blue and Maya red pigments

lead: Maya blue is a turquoise pigment made by the pre-Columbian Maya and neighbouring cultures from indigo dye bound to a fibrous clay called palygorskite. Alongside it, Maya painters used red pigments such as hematite (iron oxide) and cinnabar (mercury sulfide). The appearance payoff in antiquity was colour: vivid, long-lasting blue and red applied to murals, ceramics and, in ritual settings, to the body.

Researchers have studied the blue extensively because it resists acids, solvents and weathering. Analyses of wall paintings have identified hematite, cinnabar and indigo-based blue in the same painting palettes. Modern interest is mostly in archaeology and materials science rather than cosmetics.

paras: Archaeological and chemical studies describe Maya blue as made by heating indigo with palygorskite clay, often with incense in ritual contexts. Accounts of its use on bodies come from research on ceremonial practice at Chichen Itza. Red pigments were mineral powders used in paints and murals.

Cinnabar is mercury sulfide, and mercury compounds are toxic, so cinnabar-containing paints carry mercury exposure concerns. Maya blue is an indigo-clay material that has been studied for stability rather than as a skin product, and no cosmetic safety testing is described for it.

angle.text: These pigments gave Mesoamerican painters bright turquoise and red colour for murals, objects and ritual body painting. The blue is notable for how durable its colour is; red pigments included iron-oxide hematite and mercury-based cinnabar.

lead: Maya blue is a turquoise pigment developed in Mesoamerica from indigo dye and palygorskite clay, used from roughly the 8th century onward on murals, ceramics, sculpture and codices [1][2]. It is noted for keeping its colour under acids, alkalis and solvents [3]. In the Maya palette it sat alongside reds such as hematite and cinnabar, both identified in wall paintings at Ek' Balam [4].

For appearance, the pigments mattered as body and surface colour. Research on rituals at Chichen Itza links the blue to ceremonies in which people were covered in blue paint, and other research suggests victims of sacrifice were painted with it [1]. Red mineral pigments belonged to the same decorative tradition.
Scientists have studied Maya blue since the 1960s as an organic-inorganic hybrid; its stability is attributed to indigo binding to the clay surface and, in part, to dehydroindigo [3][5][6].
infobox: Ancient pigments (blue: indigo plus palygorskite clay)

paras: Maya blue combines indigo from the anil plant with palygorskite, a fibrous clay, and sometimes small amounts of other minerals [1]. A 1966 Science paper proposed it was an adsorption complex of the clay and natural indigo and noted it is not destroyed by hot concentrated acids [6]. Later work reported nanostructure in authentic samples, including a palygorskite superlattice and metal nanoparticle inclusions [7].

Studies using spectroscopy and electrochemistry describe the pigment as containing indigo and dehydroindigo, with indigo loading in archaeological samples estimated at about 0.2 to 1.5 percent by weight [5][8]. Researchers disagree on details such as whether indigo enters the clay's internal tunnels or sits at fibre ends [9].

Raman analysis of late Classic wall paintings from Ek' Balam identified haematite, calcite, carbon, cinnabar and indigo among the pigments used [4]. Hematite is iron oxide; cinnabar is mercury sulfide.

A 2008 study by Wheaton College researchers connected the pigment to ritual at Chichen Itza, where blue paint was made near a sacred sinkhole and people were covered in it as offerings to the rain god Chaak [1]. Other research suggests sacrificial victims were painted with it [1]. This is a ceremonial use documented by archaeologists, not a modern cosmetic.
No studies found. Research on these pigments is archaeological and materials-science work; no human skin or cosmetic trials of Maya blue or Maya reds are described.

Cinnabar contains mercury, and mercury compounds are associated with neurological and kidney harm in the toxicology literature [10]. Maya blue is an indigo-clay hybrid; published safety data concentrates on its chemical stability rather than on skin exposure.
